title: 10.2 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can use bilateral symmetry to describe structure in nature and in human creations, explain how I can tell, and judge a case I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: A butterfly rests on a leaf with its wings spread wide open. The pattern of spots and colors on the left wing repeats on the right wing.
noticeStarters: I notice the pattern of spots ___ .
I notice the butterfly's middle line is ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder why people find butterflies ___ .

turnAndTalk.question: The butterfly's two wings are mirror images across a line down the middle of its body. Why does drawing that line matter for proving the butterfly is symmetric?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A figure is symmetric only if there is a specific line where one side is a mirror image of the other.

stems.en: Drawing the line matters because it lets us ___ the two sides.
stems.es: Trazar la línea importa porque nos permite ___ los dos lados.

stems.en: The butterfly is symmetric because its two sides are ___ of each other.
stems.es: La mariposa es simétrica porque sus dos lados son ___ el uno del otro.

turnAndTalk.extend: Could a butterfly still be symmetric if its line of symmetry ran at an angle instead of straight down the middle? Justify your answer.
extendStems: Yes/No, because a line of symmetry ___.
The direction of the line ___ whether the figure is symmetric.

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted cards into 'has bilateral symmetry' and 'no bilateral symmetry,' why did the letter R end up in the 'no' column while a ladybug seen from above ended up in the 'yes' column?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The test is whether some line divides the figure into two mirror-image halves; the letter R fails that test, but a ladybug's left and right sides match.

stems.en: The letter R has no bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: La letra R no tiene simetría bilateral porque ___.

stems.en: The ladybug has bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: La mariquita tiene simetría bilateral porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: The spiral snail shell was sorted into 'no bilateral symmetry.' Could you argue it has a DIFFERENT kind of symmetry? What would you call it?
extendStems: The snail shell does not have bilateral symmetry, but it might have ___ symmetry because ___.
This is different from bilateral symmetry because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A plant grows in layers, with 2 mirror-image leaves per layer. After 4 layers, how many leaves are there, and how does that connect to bilateral symmetry?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 4 layers × 2 leaves per layer = 8 leaves, and each layer's 2 leaves are a mirror-image pair.

stems.en: After 4 layers, the plant has ___ leaves because ___.
stems.es: Después de 4 capas, la planta tiene ___ hojas porque ___.

stems.en: Each layer shows bilateral symmetry because ___.
stems.es: Cada capa muestra simetría bilateral porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: If a plant grew 6 layers instead of 4, how many leaves would it have, and would each layer still show bilateral symmetry? Explain.
extendStems: With 6 layers, the plant would have ___ leaves because ___.
Each layer would still/would not show bilateral symmetry because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when you had to decide if a figure had bilateral symmetry, what strategy helped you check it — even when the line of symmetry wasn't vertical?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A figure has bilateral symmetry if ANY line — not just a vertical one — makes the two sides mirror images.

stems.en: I checked by ___ to see if the two sides were ___.
stems.es: Comprobé al ___ para ver si los dos lados eran ___.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who assumed a line of symmetry always has to be vertical? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

vocabulary.definition: Having two halves that match — one side is a mirror image of the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Que tiene dos mitades que coinciden: un lado es la imagen reflejada del otro.
vocabulary.example: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images. The butterfly is symmetric.

vocabulary.definition: A copy of a shape flipped across a line, like a reflection in a mirror.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una copia de una figura volteada sobre una línea, como un reflejo en un espejo.
vocabulary.example: The left wing of a butterfly is a mirror image of the right wing.

vocabulary.definition: Reflective symmetry in plants and animals — the two sides of the body mirror each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La simetría reflectiva en plantas y animales: los dos lados del cuerpo se reflejan entre sí.
vocabulary.example: All butterflies have reflective symmetry; in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.

vocabulary.definition: The line you can draw through a figure so each side is a reflection of the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La línea que puedes trazar por una figura de modo que cada lado sea el reflejo del otro.
vocabulary.example: We can draw a line down the middle of the layer of leaves, along the center of each leaf.

vocabulary.definition: An even, steady arrangement — neither side feels heavier than the other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una disposición pareja y estable: ningún lado se siente más pesado que el otro.
vocabulary.example: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 10.2. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Math creates beautiful designs in nature
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Bilateral symmetry — two sides that are mirror images — appears throughout nature, and it shapes human creations from art to music to architecture — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me find the symmetry in a butterfly
lines: I look at the two sides of the butterfly, and they look like mirror images — the butterfly is symmetric.
All butterflies have reflective symmetry. In plants and animals, this is called bilateral symmetry.
To show it, I draw a line down the middle of the butterfly's body: everything on the left is reflected on the right.

explore.label: Does it have bilateral symmetry? Sort each one.

cards.text: A butterfly with wings spread open
A human face seen from the front
A layer of two leaves that are mirror images

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Test each one the same way: imagine drawing a line down the middle. If one side is a mirror image of the other, it has bilateral symmetry. After sorting, name where the line of symmetry runs on one card from the left column. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

diagram.title: Bilateral Symmetry on a Grid
diagram.caption: Plot each point, right then up; the line x = 6 acts as the line of symmetry, so every point at x = 4 has a mirror partner at x = 8 the same distance away and the two halves match.

connect.scenario: Your friend insists that only one of two flowers has bilateral symmetry. One flower's petals mirror each other across a line down its center; the other flower does too, just along a different line.
connect.promptQuestion: How do you respond to your friend?
connect.prompt: To settle the disagreement, draw a ___ through the center of each flower and check whether one side is a ___ of the other. If the test works for both, then ___ flowers have bilateral symmetry.

check.stem: A butterfly's two wings look like mirror images of each other across a line down the center of its body. What is this type of symmetry called?
check.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means one line divides a shape into two mirror-image halves, like the butterfly's wings. Rotational and radial symmetry involve a shape repeating around a center point, and point symmetry involves matching after a 180° turn — neither describes a single mirror line.

check.stem: To test whether a flower has bilateral symmetry, what should you do first?
choices: Draw a line through the center and compare the two sides
Compare the flower to a different type of flower
check.explanation: Bilateral symmetry is tested by drawing a line through the center and checking whether the two sides are mirror images. Counting petals or measuring height doesn't test whether the halves match, and comparing to a different flower doesn't test this flower's own symmetry.

check.stem: Your friend says only one of two flowers has bilateral symmetry. You test both by drawing a line through each flower's center and find both sides match on both flowers. What is most likely true?
choices: The friend is right — only one flower truly has symmetry
Both flowers have bilateral symmetry, but the second flower's line of symmetry likely runs in a direction the friend didn't try
Symmetry cannot be tested in flowers
The two flowers must be identical in shape to both be symmetric
check.explanation: Since the test showed both flowers have a line where the sides mirror each other, both are bilaterally symmetric — the friend likely only checked one direction on the second flower and missed its line of symmetry. Flowers don't need to look alike to each have their own symmetry.

connect.modelAnswer: I would tell my friend we should test both flowers the same way instead of just looking quickly. For each flower, I would draw a line through its center and check whether one side is a mirror image of the other. If both flowers pass the test, then both have bilateral symmetry — the second flower's line of symmetry might just run in a direction my friend did not try.

diagram.title: Count the steps from the fold line to each wing
diagram.caption: Fold the butterfly along 6. The left wing is 6 − 4 = 2 steps from the fold, and the right wing is 8 − 6 = 2 steps. Equal steps on both sides is what makes it symmetric — if one side were 3 steps, the halves would not match.

onLevel.stem: Why do people find symmetry pleasing?
choices: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance
Symmetric things are always brightly colored
Symmetry only appears in rare and expensive objects
Symmetric shapes are always larger than non-symmetric ones
onLevel.explanation: The lesson says it directly: our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.
choiceFeedback: Color is separate from symmetry — a plain gray moth can be perfectly symmetric.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature, from leaves to ladybugs — it is common, not rare.
Size has nothing to do with it — a tiny symmetric leaf is as balanced as a huge one.
hints: This asks two things: which box holds more AND by how many cubic inches — so find both volumes first.
Compute each volume with V = l × w × h, then subtract the smaller total from the larger.
Box A: 10 × 5 = 50, then × 4. Box B: 8 × 6 = 48, then × 5. Compare the two totals.
onLevel.stemEs: Dos cajas: la caja A mide 10 × 5 × 4 pulgadas. La caja B mide 8 × 6 × 5 pulgadas. ¿Cuál tiene más volumen y por cuánto?
onLevel.explanationEs: Caja A: 10 × 5 × 4 = 200 in³. Caja B: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. La caja B es mayor por 40 in³.
hintsEs: Esto pregunta dos cosas: cuál caja guarda más Y por cuántas pulgadas cúbicas, así que halla primero ambos volúmenes.
Calcula cada volumen con V = l × a × h y luego resta el total menor del mayor.
Caja A: 10 × 5 = 50 y luego × 4. Caja B: 8 × 6 = 48 y luego × 5. Compara los dos totales.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: A box is 6 in long, 4 in wide, and 1/2 in tall.

workedExample.label: Calculate
workedExample.work: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2, and the student dropped the 1/2: V = 6 × 4 = 24 cubic in

onLevel.correctWork: The student ignored the fractional edge of 1/2 in. A fractional edge still counts: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in.
hints: Check Step 3: did the student use the 1/2 in height in the multiplication?
A fractional edge does not change the rule. Multiply all three: 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in, not 24.
onLevel.explanation: The Calculate step threw away the 1/2 in height, but a fractional edge is still an edge. Multiply all three: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in. A half-inch height makes the volume half of 24, not equal to it.
onLevel.explanationEs: En el paso de calcular se descartó la altura de 1/2 in, pero un lado fraccionario sigue siendo un lado. Multiplica los tres: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 pulgadas cúbicas. Una altura de media pulgada hace que el volumen sea la mitad de 24, no igual a 24.

The answer is about how our brains respond.
What does bilateral symmetry provide that brains favor?
Think of an even, steady arrangement.

practice.stem: There are over 17,000 species of butterflies, and ALL butterflies have reflective symmetry. About how many of those species have reflective symmetry?
choices: None — symmetry is only in plants
practice.explanation: 'All butterflies have reflective symmetry' means every one of the 17,000+ species — no exceptions.
choiceFeedback: 'All' means every single species, not half of them.
Symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about how colorful the wings are.
The butterfly itself was our first example — animals show bilateral symmetry too.
hints: One edge is a fraction: 1/2 m. The other edges are 3 m and 4 m. The formula works the same with fractions.
Multiply all three edges: V = 1/2 × 3 × 4. Multiplying by 1/2 is the same as dividing by 2.
Multiply the whole numbers first: 3 × 4 = 12. Then take half of that result.
practice.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el volumen de un prisma con longitudes de arista de 1/2 m, 3 m y 4 m?
hintsEs: Una arista es una fracción: 1/2 m. Las otras aristas son 3 m y 4 m. La fórmula funciona igual con fracciones.
Multiplica las tres aristas: V = 1/2 × 3 × 4. Multiplicar por 1/2 es lo mismo que dividir entre 2.
Multiplica primero los números enteros: 3 × 4 = 12. Luego saca la mitad de ese resultado.
One edge is a fraction: 1/2 m. The other edges are 3 m and 4 m. The formula works the same with fractions.
Multiply all three edges: V = 1/2 × 3 × 4. Multiplying by 1/2 is the same as dividing by 2.
Multiply the whole numbers first: 3 × 4 = 12. Then take half of that result.
practice.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el volumen de un prisma con longitudes de arista de 1/2 m, 3 m y 4 m?
practice.explanationEs: Read the statement carefully: ALL butterflies.

stem: Are the two leaves in a real plant layer EXACTLY symmetric? Why might this be?
modelAnswer: No — the leaves are close to mirror images but not exact. Real plants grow in messy conditions: one leaf might get more sun or get nibbled by an insect, so the two sides come out slightly different. Nature follows the pattern of bilateral symmetry without being perfect.

stem: A plant grows 2 leaves at a time, one layer per week. How many leaves has it grown after 6 weeks?
explanation: One layer per week for 6 weeks is 6 layers, and 6 layers × 2 leaves = 12 leaves.
choiceFeedback: 8 comes from adding 6 + 2 instead of multiplying.
6 counts the layers but forgets each layer holds 2 leaves.
36 squares the 6 weeks (6 × 6) instead of multiplying weeks by leaves per layer.
hints: A cube's edges are all equal, so its length, width, and height are each 5 cm.
Use V = edge × edge × edge — multiply 5 by itself three times, not 5 × 3.
Start with 5 × 5 = 25, then multiply that result by 5 one more time.
stemEs: Un cubo tiene una longitud de arista de 5 cm. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
explanationEs: El volumen de un cubo es arista³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.
hintsEs: Las aristas de un cubo son todas iguales, así que su largo, ancho y altura son 5 cm cada uno.
Usa V = arista × arista × arista: multiplica 5 por sí mismo tres veces, no 5 × 3.
Empieza con 5 × 5 = 25 y luego multiplica ese resultado por 5 una vez más.

Use V = edge × edge × edge — multiply 5 by itself three times, not 5 × 3.
Start with 5 × 5 = 25, then multiply that result by 5 one more time.

explanationEs: El volumen de un cubo es arista³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.
How many layers grow in 6 weeks?
Each layer is made up of 2 leaves.

extending.stem: Where else do you see bilateral symmetry — in nature OR in something humans made?
extending.modelAnswer: I see bilateral symmetry in the front of my school building: the doors are in the center, and the windows on the left side mirror the windows on the right side. The line of symmetry runs straight down through the middle of the doors.

extending.stem: Which is the best test for whether a figure has bilateral symmetry?
choices: Find a line where one side is the mirror image of the other
Check whether the figure has an even number of parts
Check whether the figure is found in nature
Check whether the figure looks beautiful to you
extending.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means exactly this: there is a line across which the two sides are mirror images.
choiceFeedback: An even number of parts is not enough — the letter Z has 2 matching ends but no mirror line.
Humans create bilateral symmetry too, in art, music, and architecture — nature is not required.
Beauty is an opinion; the mirror-image test gives the same answer no matter who runs it.
hints: Go back to the definition, not the feeling.
What must exist for the two sides to reflect across?
Mirror image across a line.

extending.prompt: A toy company ships action figures in boxes that are 4 × 3 × 6 inches. A shipping crate is 24 × 12 × 18 inches. How many action figure boxes fit in the crate? Explain your reasoning step by step.
extending.sentenceFrame: Each toy box has a volume of ___ in³. The crate has a volume of ___ in³. I can fit ___ boxes because ___. I checked by ___.
extending.hint: Find three different factor combinations of the target volume.
hints: Two sizes matter: each toy box is 4 × 3 × 6 in and the crate is 24 × 12 × 18 in. Each crate edge is a multiple of a box edge.
Find both volumes, then divide the crate's volume by one box's volume. Check by counting rows, columns, and layers.
Start with one toy box: multiply 4 × 3 = 12, then multiply by 6. Next find the crate's volume the same way.
extending.explanation: Each toy box holds 4 × 3 × 6 = 72 in³ and the crate holds 24 × 12 × 18 = 5184 in³, so 5184 ÷ 72 = 72 boxes fit. The division comes out exact because every crate edge is a whole-number multiple of a box edge: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 across, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 deep, and 18 ÷ 6 = 3 layers, and 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 confirms it.
extending.explanationEs: Cada caja de juguete tiene 4 × 3 × 6 = 72 in³ y la caja grande tiene 24 × 12 × 18 = 5184 in³, así que caben 5184 ÷ 72 = 72 cajas. La división sale exacta porque cada lado de la caja grande es un múltiplo entero de un lado de la caja pequeña: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 a lo ancho, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 de fondo y 18 ÷ 6 = 3 capas, y 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 lo confirma.
extending.promptEs: Una juguetería envía figuras de acción en cajas de 4 × 3 × 6 pulgadas. Una caja de embarque mide 24 × 12 × 18 pulgadas. ¿Cuántas cajas de figuras caben en la caja de embarque? Explica tu razonamiento paso a paso.
hintsEs: Importan dos tamaños: cada caja de juguetes mide 4 × 3 × 6 pulg y el cajón mide 24 × 12 × 18 pulg. Cada arista del cajón es múltiplo de una arista de la caja.
Halla ambos volúmenes y luego divide el volumen del cajón entre el de una caja. Compruébalo contando filas, columnas y capas.
Empieza con una caja de juguetes: multiplica 4 × 3 = 12 y luego multiplica por 6. Después halla el volumen del cajón igual.

extending.stem: A fish tank measures 2 1/2 ft by 2 ft by 3 ft. What is its volume?
choiceFeedback: You multiplied two dimensions but left out the third edge length.
Check the fractional edge length — rounding it down changes your answer.
Double check your multiplication — recompute each step to avoid doubling the result.
hints: One dimension is a mixed number: 2 1/2 ft. Rewrite it as 2.5 before multiplying.
Use V = l × w × h with all three numbers: 2.5 × 2 × 3. Keep the half — don't round it away.
Multiply the easy pair first: 2 × 3 = 6. Then multiply that result by 2.5.
extending.stemEs: Una pecera mide 2 1/2 ft por 2 ft por 3 ft. ¿Cuál es su volumen?

extending.stem: A prism with a 3/4 ft by 2 ft base has a volume of 9 ft³. What is its height?
choiceFeedback: Recalculate the base area first (3/4 × 2), then divide the volume by that.
That's the volume given, not the height — divide it by the base area to find height.
Make sure you find the full base area — multiply both base dimensions before dividing.
hints: You know the volume (9 ft³) and the base dimensions (3/4 ft and 2 ft). The height is missing.
Height = Volume ÷ base area. Find the base area first, then divide the volume by it.
Base area: 3/4 × 2 = 1.5 ft². Now ask what number times 1.5 equals 9.
extending.stemEs: Un prisma con una base de 3/4 ft por 2 ft tiene un volumen de 9 ft³. ¿Cuál es su altura?
extending.explanationEs: Altura = V ÷ (área de la base) = 9 ÷ (3/4 × 2) = 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 ft.
hintsEs: Conoces el volumen (9 pies³) y las dimensiones de la base (3/4 pie y 2 pies). Falta la altura.
Altura = Volumen ÷ área de la base. Halla primero el área de la base y luego divide el volumen entre ella.
Área de la base: 3/4 × 2 = 1.5 pies². Ahora pregunta qué número por 1.5 da 9.

extending.stem: A time-capsule box measures 6 in long, 4 in wide, and 3 in tall. What is its volume?
extending.explanation: V = length × width × height = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 cubic in. Volume uses cubic units.
choiceFeedback: Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
You multiplied two dimensions but forgot the third — include length, width, AND height.
Check the units — this fills 3D space, so it needs cubic units, not square units.
extending.stemEs: Una caja para una cápsula del tiempo mide 6 in de largo, 4 in de ancho y 3 in de alto. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
extending.explanationEs: V = largo × ancho × alto = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 pulgadas cúbicas. El volumen usa unidades cúbicas.
hints: Volume measures the space inside a solid, and it is always labeled in cubic units.
Use V = length × width × height: multiply two of the dimensions first, then multiply by the third.
Start with 6 × 4 = 24. Now multiply that result by the height of 3.
hintsEs: El volumen mide el espacio dentro de un cuerpo y siempre se escribe en unidades cúbicas.
Usa V = largo × ancho × alto: multiplica primero dos de las dimensiones y luego multiplica por la tercera.
Empieza con 6 × 4 = 24. Ahora multiplica ese resultado por la altura de 3.

hintsEs: El volumen mide el espacio dentro de un cuerpo y siempre se escribe en unidades cúbicas.
Usa V = largo × ancho × alto: multiplica primero dos de las dimensiones y luego multiplica por la tercera.
Empieza con 6 × 4 = 24. Ahora multiplica ese resultado por la altura de 3.
hintsEs.stem: The lesson says bilateral symmetry influences human creations 'from art to music to architecture.' Pick ONE of those three and describe how symmetry appears in it.
hintsEs.modelAnswer: In architecture, many famous buildings are designed with bilateral symmetry: the entrance sits in the exact center, and every column or window on the left has a matching one on the right. Architects use that balance on purpose because our brains are wired to favor it.

hintsEs.stem: Your friend insists that only ONE of two flowers has bilateral symmetry, but both pass the mirror-image test — just across lines pointing in different directions. What is the best response?
choices: Both flowers have bilateral symmetry — a line of symmetry does not have to point the same direction in every figure
Your friend is right, because a real line of symmetry must always be vertical
Neither flower has bilateral symmetry, because flowers are not animals
Agree with your friend, because two people should not disagree about math
hintsEs.explanation: The test for bilateral symmetry is whether SOME line makes the two sides mirror images — the direction of that line does not matter.
choiceFeedback: Nothing in the definition requires vertical — a mirror line can run in any direction.
Plants have bilateral symmetry too; the leaf layers in this very lesson were the example.
Math disagreements are settled with evidence and a test, not with politeness.
hints: How much a box holds is its volume, not its height or its widest side.
Find the volume of each box separately with V = l × w × h, then compare the two numbers.
For Box A, 5 × 5 = 25, then multiply by 2. Do the same kind of work for Box B before comparing.

Halla el volumen de cada caja por separado con V = l × w × h y luego compara los dos números.

choicesEs: La caja A, porque 50 pulgadas cúbicas es más que 48 pulgadas cúbicas
La caja B, porque 48 pulgadas cúbicas es más que 50 pulgadas cúbicas
La caja B, porque es más alta

hintsEs.stem: You and a friend are studying a building for an art project. The building's left half mirrors its right half. What can you say about the building in terms of bilateral symmetry?
hintsEs.modelAnswer: The building has bilateral symmetry: I can draw a vertical line of symmetry down its center, and every window, column, and door on the left is a mirror image of one on the right. The architects designed it that way on purpose — humans design for beauty using bilateral symmetry, because that balance is pleasing to our brains.

hintsEs.stem: A symmetric garden design puts the same planting on each side of a center path. One side uses 14 tulips and 9 daisies. How many flowers does the WHOLE symmetric design use?
hintsEs.explanation: One side uses 14 + 9 = 23 flowers, and the mirror side uses the same 23, so the whole design uses 23 × 2 = 46 flowers.
choiceFeedback: 23 is just ONE side — bilateral symmetry means the other side matches it, doubling the total.
28 doubles only the tulips (14 × 2) and forgets to double the 9 daisies.
126 multiplies 14 × 9 — but the two flower counts should be added, then doubled.
hints: A fractional edge length works exactly like a whole-number one — the formula V = l × w × h does not change.
Multiply the two whole-number edges first, then multiply that product by the fractional height.
4 × 3 = 12. Now multiply 12 by 1½, which you can split into 12 × 1 plus 12 × ½.

hintsEs.stem: The lesson says math CREATES the beautiful designs we find in nature. Someone argues back: 'Nature is beautiful, but that has nothing to do with math.' Use the butterfly, the plant, or symmetry in your answer to respond.
hintsEs.modelAnswer: I would say the beauty and the math are the same thing. What makes a butterfly's wings so striking is that the two sides are exact mirror images — that is bilateral symmetry, a mathematical structure. The plant grows its leaves two at a time in mirrored pairs. Our brains are wired to favor balance, so when we call nature beautiful, we are often responding to the math inside it without naming it.
sentenceStems: The math inside the beauty is ___ .

hintsEs.stem: What does it mean that a butterfly is symmetric?
choices: The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images
The butterfly has exactly two wings
The butterfly's wings are very colorful
The butterfly is larger than most insects
hintsEs.explanation: Symmetric means one side is a mirror image of the other — that is exactly what we see across the butterfly's body.
choiceFeedback: Having two wings is not enough — the two sides must MIRROR each other to be symmetric.
Color makes a butterfly pretty, but symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about color.
Size has nothing to do with symmetry — a tiny butterfly is just as symmetric as a big one.
hints: Think about what you see on the left wing versus the right wing.
Imagine a mirror standing along the butterfly's body.
What word describes two sides that reflect each other?

extending.commonMistake: Thinking a figure lacks bilateral symmetry just because its line of symmetry is not vertical — the mirror line can run in any direction, and the test is whether the two sides match across it.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Which statement best shows what this lesson means by 'math is beauty'?
choices: Math creates beautiful designs like bilateral symmetry, found in nature and used in human art, music, and architecture
Only things made by mathematicians can be beautiful
Butterflies are the only living things with symmetry
Beauty and math are opposites — one is feeling and one is numbers
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes the claim in two parts: bilateral symmetry appears naturally in many plants and animals, and it also influences human creations from art to music to architecture.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It mentions nature AND human creations.
Which option includes both?

questions.stem: What is the volume of a rectangular prism with l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in?
questions.explanation: V = l × w × h = 7 × 3 × 4 = 84 cubic inches.

questions.stem: Which unit is used for volume?
questions.explanation: Volume measures 3D space, so it uses cubic units like in³. Square units (in²) are for area, and inches are for length.

questions.stem: A time capsule box has a volume of 120 cm³. Its length is 10 cm and width is 4 cm. What is its height?
